payload.acceptance_criteria: the reason is on this record and reachable from the release process, so the next reader meets the argument before the change; release.PIN_GLOBS still names only docs/how-to
payload.description:
When a release refuses because the tutorial names the old version, I want the reason written down, so I can stop someone adding docs/tutorial to the pin globs and quietly falsifying a transcript.

docs/tutorial/first-loop.md opens by claiming every command and every quoted output was executed in a real terminal on a named version. docs-claims enforces that the named version is the newest released one, so a release refuses until the page is re-recorded. That refusal is the gate working.

Adding docs/tutorial to release.PIN_GLOBS looks like the obvious fix and is the wrong one. The pin pattern matches the @vX.Y.Z install line, which is a command, but the page also carries engine: basicly X.Y.Z inside recorded output. Rewriting those would make the opening sentence false while the gate went green. I made that change during v0.14.0 and reverted it.
payload.requirements: no gate is weakened and no waiver is added: the release stays refused until a human re-records the page
payload.title: record why the tutorial is not a release pin target

payload.text:
Re-recorded for v0.14.0 on 2026-09-18. A fresh git repository, basicly installed from a locally built 0.14.0 wheel, then every step of the page walked: install, status, gitignore, policy scaffold, tracker create, policy dor, the install commit, loop status, loop run to the classify checkpoint, the worktree edit and its commit, the landing, the ship approval, git log and the closing loop status.

Every quoted block matched what the page already said apart from ids, commit hashes and sub-second timings. basicly status was identical field for field. The six commits came out in the same shapes and the same order. So the five version strings were the only edit the page needed, and the opening sentence is true.

Two things the recording had to route around, neither a page defect. The shell is not a TTY, so a checkpoint prints a one-time code rather than taking the terminal as the human - which the page already documents as the relay. And loop run --confirm refuses the ship checkpoint whatever code it is given, because the advance reissues the code before reading it; policy checkpoint <id> ship --approve --confirm is the surface that works. The page never shows either, because a reader at a terminal meets neither.

A structural fact that decides how this can ever be done: basicly release tags locally and deliberately does not push, so @vX.Y.Z is unreachable until after the release. The page can only be recorded against a locally built engine, with the git+ line as the documented equivalent.

payload.name: close_reason
payload.value: recorded: the tutorial is deliberately not a pin target, and the v0.14.0 re-recording is on the record with what it could not reproduce and why
